## The question

[How am I incorrectly solving this polar equations graph?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2271596/how-am-i-incorrectly-solving-this-polar-equations-graph), asked by [yre](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/428730/yre) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-05-08; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> >Graph: $r = 1 + 2\cos(\theta)$
>
> I set up a table of values and increment them by $π/2$:
>
> $$\begin{array}
> {|c|c|}\hline
> \phantom{\_\_\_}\theta\phantom{\_\_\_} &  \phantom{\_\_\_}r\phantom{\_\_\_} \\ \hline
> 0      &  3 \\ \hline
> \pi/2  &  1 \\ \hline
> \pi    & -1 \\ \hline
> 3\pi/2 &  1 \\ \hline
> 2\pi   &  3 \\ \hline
> 5\pi/2 &  1 \\ \hline
> 3\pi   & -1 \\ \hline
> 7\pi/2 &  1 \\ \hline
> 4\pi   &  3 \\ \hline
> \end{array}$$
>
> When I plot these points I get:
>
> [![enter image description here][q-1]][q-1]
>
> When I go about graphing I think of $\theta$ as direction, and $r$ as distance. So I point in a direction, and go a certain distance. Then to the next one and I connect the dots. But there seems to be more going on than just connecting the dots when I look at the actual graph on Desmos. How am I supposed to know it's going to loop inwards, go through the $y$-axis, and go back to $1$ on the $x$-axis?
> Actual:
>
> [![enter image description here][q-2]][q-2]
>
>
> Thank you
>
>
>   [q-1]: J5fZs.png
>   [q-2]: 1l2Iu.png
:::

One way to see that the polar curve loops inward is to graph $r$ versus $\theta$ on cartesian axes.  You see that $r$ becomes negative when $\cos\theta < -\frac{1}{2}$; that is on the interval $\left(\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)$.
